Scan plants, diagnose disease & get care tips
Use clean, disease-free seeds and fresh soil. Always disinfect your tools before use.
Don’t overcrowd your plants. Proper spacing keeps leaves dry and reduces fungus.
Isolate the affected plant to prevent the pest from spreading. Consider using organic pest control methods like neem oil or insecticidal soap based on the pest type.
Never refrigerate unripe tomatoes; keep them stem-down on the counter away from direct sunlight.

Receive timely reminders to water and care for your plants.
Cut off any spotted or damaged leaves immediately — it stops the spread fast.
Only water at the soil level. Wet leaves make the infection worse.
Apply diatomaceous earth around the plant base. Use bait traps and remove plant debris. Keep the soil surface clean to discourage nesting.
Bees are essential pollinators — do not kill them. If a hive is too close, contact a local beekeeper in your area for safe relocation.
Hand-pick beetles in early morning when they are sluggish. Apply neem oil spray weekly. Use row covers on young transplants to prevent access.
Apply Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spray, which is organic and widely available in Pakistan. Hand-pick visible caterpillars. Encourage parasitic wasps by planting dill or fennel nearby.
Earthworms are highly beneficial — they aerate soil and improve fertility. No action needed. Their presence indicates healthy soil.
Set traps using damp rolled newspaper placed near plants overnight. Remove garden debris and mulch piles where earwigs hide during the day.
Use floating row covers to protect crops. Apply neem oil or Nosema locustae bait for biological control. Remove weeds around field borders where they breed.
Use pheromone traps to monitor and reduce moth populations. Apply Bt spray to control larvae. Inspect leaf undersides regularly and remove egg clusters.
Set beer traps (shallow containers filled with beer) near affected plants. Apply iron phosphate bait pellets. Create copper tape barriers around pots or raised beds.
Hand-pick snails during early morning or after rain. Use iron phosphate bait. Apply copper tape around stems and containers to create an electric barrier.
Wasps are beneficial predators that eat caterpillars and aphids. Avoid disturbing nests unless they are dangerously close to work areas. Relocate if necessary.
Apply neem oil to foliage. Use sticky traps around plant stems. Remove and destroy heavily infested plant parts. Rotate crops to break the lifecycle.
Unable to determine pest type. Please retake the photo with clearer lighting and ensure the pest is fully visible in the frame.

Harvest immediately and store at room temperature, stem-side down, out of direct sunlight. Do not refrigerate — cold temperatures destroy flavor and cause a mealy texture. For Pakistani markets, harvest in early morning when the fruit is cool. Use within 3–5 days for best quality.

Leave the tomato on the vine for 5–10 more days until it shows full color. If temperatures exceed 35°C, harvest at the breaker stage (first hint of pink) and ripen indoors at 20–25°C. Avoid direct sunlight during indoor ripening.
Unable to determine ripeness stage. Ensure the photo clearly shows the tomato surface with natural lighting. Try cropping the image to focus only on the fruit, removing any background leaves or soil.
Prune and destroy lower leaves showing target-like brown spots with concentric rings. Do not compost infected debris.
Spray Mancozeb or Saaf (Carbendazim + Mancozeb), widely available in Pakistan. Apply every 7–10 days during humid weather. Rotate with copper-based fungicides.
Continue watering at the base, not on foliage. Ensure proper spacing between plants for air circulation.
Apply a preventive copper spray during monsoon season. Rotate crops every 2–3 years and keep the garden free of weeds.
Remove and destroy all infected leaves, stems, and fruits immediately. Late blight spreads rapidly in cool, wet conditions (18–22°C).
Spray Ridomil Gold (Metalaxyl + Mancozeb) or Curzate M. These are widely available from agricultural dealers in Pakistan. Start treatment at first symptoms.
Strip infected lower leaves showing small spots with gray centers and dark borders. Look for tiny black dots (pycnidia) in spot centers.
Mulch around plant base with wheat straw to prevent rain splashing spores onto leaves. Apply Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb every 7 days during wet spells.
Ensure the leaf is well-lit, in focus, and fills most of the frame for accurate diagnosis.
Water at the base, maintain proper spacing, and monitor leaves daily for any changes in color or texture.

No scans yet. Use the scanner to diagnose your first plant!
Your plant has Early Blight. You will see brown spots with ring patterns on the lower leaves. It happens more in hot and humid weather.
Pick off the spotted leaves right away and throw them in the trash. Spray the healthy leaves with copper fungicide and spray again after it rains. Water the soil only — do not wet the leaves.
Always water at the base, never from above. Put mulch around the plant to stop soil from splashing up. Do not grow tomatoes in the same spot every year. Cut off any low branches touching the ground.
Great news! Your plant looks healthy. No disease found. Keep doing what you are doing and check your plants often.
No treatment needed right now. Keep checking leaves every week, especially after rainy days.
Water at the base regularly and keep plants spaced apart for good air flow. Add fertilizer once a month. Cut lower branches that touch the soil and check under the leaves every week.
Your plant has Late Blight. This is a serious disease that spreads fast. You will see dark watery spots on leaves, sometimes with white mold underneath.

Act fast! Remove all sick leaves and branches now. Spray copper fungicide on the healthy parts. If most of the plant is sick, pull out the whole plant, put it in a bag and throw it away. Do not compost.

Do not plant in areas that stay wet and cool. Keep plants spaced apart and use stakes. Clean up all dead plant parts at end of season. Water early in the morning so leaves dry fast. Check plants every day when weather is cool and rainy.
Your plant has Septoria Leaf Spot. You will see small round spots with light centers and dark edges on the lower leaves. Leaves may turn yellow and fall off.
Cut off all spotted leaves and throw them away. Spray copper fungicide on the remaining healthy leaves and spray again after rain. Do not touch plants when leaves are wet.
Always water at the base, never spray from above. Clean up all dead plants at end of season. Do not grow tomatoes in the same spot for 2–3 years. Use stakes to keep leaves off the ground.
We could not identify the problem clearly. Try scanning again with better light, or ask a local farming expert for help.
Look closely at the plant for any spots or color changes. If you see something wrong, remove those leaves. Watch the plant for a few days to see if it gets worse.
Water at the base and keep plants spaced apart. Add fertilizer and remove weeds regularly. Do not grow the same crop in the same spot every year. Check your plants often for any changes.
Late Blight thrives on wet leaves. Aim the can at the soil, not the foliage.
Tomatoes need full sun. Less than 6 hours weakens defenses against disease.
Cut leaves touching the soil. They are the first to catch fungal spores.
Your plant has Bacterial Spot. Look for small water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown or black, with raised scabby spots on green fruits. It spreads fast in warm wet weather.
Remove and destroy infected leaves and fruits — do not compost them. Spray copper-based bactericide every 7–10 days. Avoid working in the garden when plants are wet to stop the spread.
Use certified disease-free seeds. Rotate tomato plots every 2–3 years. Water at the base only and stake plants to keep foliage dry. Sterilize pruning tools between plants.
Your plant has Bacterial Canker. You will see one-sided wilting, brown leaf edges, and small white \"bird\'s-eye\" spots on the fruit. It often enters through pruning wounds.
There is no cure once a plant is infected. Pull out and destroy the whole plant to protect the rest. Disinfect stakes, cages, and tools with bleach. Spray neighbors with copper as a precaution.
Buy seeds and transplants from trusted sources. Avoid pruning when plants are wet. Sanitize all tools between plants. Do not save seeds from infected fields.
Your plant has Bacterial Wilt. The plant suddenly wilts and dies even though leaves stay green. Cut the stem and you will see a milky ooze coming out — that is the bacteria.
There is no chemical cure. Remove infected plants right away and burn or bag them. Do not plant tomatoes, peppers, eggplants, or potatoes in the same spot for at least 3 years.
Plant resistant varieties when available. Use raised beds with well-drained soil. Avoid wounding roots while weeding. Rotate crops with grasses or legumes for 3+ years.
Your plant has Mosaic Virus. Leaves show a mottled pattern of light and dark green, often with curling and stunted growth. Fruits may be small and discolored.
There is no cure. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to stop the spread. Wash hands and tools with soap before touching healthy plants. Tobacco users must wash hands extra carefully.
Use certified virus-free seeds. Control aphids and whiteflies which spread the virus. Do not smoke or handle tobacco near tomato plants. Disinfect tools with milk or 10% bleach.
Your plant has Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus. Leaves curl upward, turn yellow at the edges, and growth is severely stunted. It is spread by whiteflies.
No cure exists. Remove infected plants and destroy them in sealed bags. Treat surviving plants for whiteflies using yellow sticky traps and insecticidal soap or neem oil.
Plant resistant varieties (TYLCV-resistant). Use reflective mulch to repel whiteflies. Cover seedlings with fine mesh until flowering. Remove weeds that host the virus.
Your plant has Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus. You will see bronze or purple spots on leaves, dark streaks on stems, and ringspots on fruit. It is spread by tiny insects called thrips.
No cure exists. Remove and destroy infected plants. Control thrips with blue sticky traps and spinosad-based insecticide. Check nearby ornamentals which often host the virus.
Use TSWV-resistant tomato varieties. Keep weeds and flowering plants away from the tomato bed. Use reflective mulch. Cover transplants with row covers for the first 4 weeks.
Your plant has Powdery Mildew. White or gray powder appears on leaf surfaces, often on the upper side. Leaves may yellow and drop. It thrives in warm dry days with cool humid nights.
Spray a mix of 1 teaspoon baking soda + a few drops dish soap in 1 liter water on affected leaves weekly. Or use sulfur-based or potassium bicarbonate fungicides. Remove badly infected leaves.
Space plants for good air flow. Water in the morning at the base. Avoid heavy nitrogen fertilizers. Plant resistant varieties and prune low branches to improve air circulation.
Your plant has Anthracnose. Ripe fruits develop small sunken circular spots that grow and turn dark. The spots may have black dots in the center. It mostly attacks ripe fruit in wet weather.
Pick and destroy all infected fruits — do not let them fall to the soil. Spray copper or chlorothalonil fungicide every 7–10 days as fruits ripen. Harvest ripe fruit promptly.
Mulch around plants to prevent soil splashing onto fruit. Rotate crops every 3 years. Stake or cage plants so fruit does not touch the ground. Pick fruit at the breaker stage during wet spells.
Your plant has Fusarium Wilt. Lower leaves yellow and wilt — often only on one side of the plant. Cut the stem and you will see brown streaks inside. The plant dies slowly.
There is no cure. Remove infected plants and destroy them. The fungus stays in soil for many years, so do not plant tomatoes or related crops there for 5+ years.
Plant resistant varieties (look for VFN labels on seed packets). Keep soil pH between 6.5 and 7. Avoid heavy nitrogen. Solarize soil during hot months by covering with clear plastic for 6 weeks.
Your plant has Verticillium Wilt. You will see V-shaped yellow patches on lower leaves, wilting on hot afternoons but recovering at night, and brown streaks inside the stem.
No effective treatment. Remove infected plants. Keep remaining plants well-watered to reduce stress. Harvest what you can before the plant dies completely.
Plant resistant varieties (V on seed labels). Rotate with non-host crops like corn or beans for 4+ years. Solarize soil. Avoid planting after potatoes, peppers, or eggplants.
Your plant has Gray Mold (Botrytis). Look for fuzzy gray growth on dying leaves, stems, flowers, and fruit. It spreads in cool, damp, still air — especially in greenhouses.
Cut off all moldy parts and bag them — do not shake or you will spread spores. Improve air flow with fans or pruning. Spray with a biological fungicide containing Bacillus subtilis.
Space plants well and prune lower leaves. Water early in the day so foliage dries fast. Remove dead flowers and fallen fruit. Heat or ventilate greenhouses to reduce humidity below 85%.
You are looking at Aphids. These are tiny soft-bodied insects (green, black, or yellow) that cluster under leaves and on new growth. They suck sap and spread viruses.
Spray plants with strong water jet to knock aphids off. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil weekly until gone. Release ladybugs or lacewings as natural predators.
Inspect new transplants before bringing them home. Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen. Plant marigolds, garlic, or chives nearby as repellents. Encourage beneficial insects with diverse flowers.
Check leaves, stems, and fruit every day during the growing season. Early action stops most problems.
Clean pruners and stakes with diluted bleach between plants to prevent spreading pathogens.
